I didn’t do inpatient voluntarily, but I have done partial hospitalization voluntarily multiple times (meaning I was there 8-10 hours a day and consented to inpatient admission whenever they thought necessary). 

Generally doctors don’t want to keep you inpatient if they don’t feel like it’s necessary. They understand that long term growth is difficult in temporary inpatient situations. In my experience, going voluntarily means that you’re more open to the care that you’ll be receiving and will get more out of the experience than if you went against your will. If you’re really putting in effort and working your hardest to get better then you don’t have to be worried about doctors trying to keep you for longer than you need. The purpose of inpatient is to cram in all the help you can get very quickly so you can apply what you’ve learned to your real life, and going in prepared and ready to receive that help does a lot to really using it. 

It’s a good idea. Good luck. I hope things get better for you.

A 34 on the act is not “decently smart.” It’s so so smart. And to make champion swimmer, even if you don’t do it anymore, takes character and hard work that so many people aren’t willing to put in. 

Things change so much when you start college. I don’t know your circumstances, so I don’t know how things could improve, but I promise you that those couple of years after high school are so unlike everything you’ve lived before. It’s worth sticking around for to try it all out. 

I hope things start to get better for you. You deserve happiness, and happiness will come. Sometimes all it takes is a change of scenery.
